notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to both Moses and Aaron to begin a new count of the Levites. The earlier census counted every male from one month old, but this one focuses only on those ready for active labor. Aaron was included because the priests had to supervise the Levites in handling the holy things.

God commanded a census of the Kohathite clan by their families. Even though Gershon was Levi's firstborn son, Kohath was listed first because his descendants carried the most sacred furnishings of the sanctuary. God ordered the work according to the holiness of the items, not by human birth order.

Only men between thirty and fifty years old were chosen for this work. These years were viewed as the prime of life, providing the physical strength and mature judgment needed to carry heavy, sacred loads. The Hebrew word for this service compares it to military duty, showing that tabernacle work was treated as a sacred warfare.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition notes the ancient Greek translation gives the starting age as twenty-five, explaining that Levites began five years of training before taking on full service at thirty.

notes.meaning: The special assignment of the Kohathites was to transport the most holy objects from the Tent of Meeting. This included the ark of the covenant, the golden altars, the lampstand, and the table of the Presence. Because these furnishings were so sacred, carrying them was both a high honor and a grave responsibility.

Before the camp set out, Aaron and his sons had to go inside and take down the inner curtain separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. They used this curtain to cover the ark of the Testimony so that no one else would see it. Normal rules kept ordinary priests out of that room, but an exception was made when the camp prepared to move.

Over the inner curtain, the priests placed a protective layer of fine leather and then a cloth of solid blue. This blue cloth made the ark stand out from every other piece of furniture while Israel marched. Finally, they adjusted the carrying poles so the ark could be carried on men's shoulders without being touched.

The table for the bread of the Presence was covered with a blue cloth, and its dishes, cups, and bowls were placed on top. The sacred bread remained on the table even during travel, showing God's constant presence with His people. The priests then placed a scarlet cloth over everything, added a protective leather cover, and inserted the carrying poles.

The golden lampstand and all its tools, including wicks, trays, and oil jars, were wrapped in a blue cloth. These items were then enclosed in fine leather and placed on a wooden carrying frame. This allowed the workers to lift and transport the lampstand safely without touching the sacred metal.

The gold altar of incense, which stood inside the Holy Place, was also covered with a blue cloth and wrapped in fine leather. After wrapping it securely, the priests put its carrying poles in place. This kept the precious golden altar safe from desert weather and hidden from common view.

All the smaller tools used for ministry in the sanctuary were gathered and wrapped together. They were placed in a blue cloth, covered in protective leather, and set on a carrying frame. Wrapping these articles showed deep reverence and kept them from being damaged during travel.

The bronze altar of burnt offering in the outer courtyard had to be cleared of ashes before being covered with a purple cloth. All its tools, such as firepans, meat forks, shovels, and basins, were placed on top of it. A layer of protective leather was spread over the whole altar, and its carrying poles were inserted.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient Greek and Samaritan versions include instructions here for wrapping the bronze washbasin, which is not mentioned in the traditional Hebrew text.

notes.meaning: Only after the priests finished wrapping every sacred object could the Kohathites come to carry them. They had to carry the items by the poles and were strictly forbidden to touch the holy things directly. Touching an uncovered holy object would result in death, showing how seriously God's holiness was to be honored.

Eleazar, the eldest surviving son of Aaron, was given personal charge over the tabernacle and its consumable supplies. He watched over the lamp oil, the fragrant incense, the regular grain offerings, and the holy anointing oil. He also supervised the Kohathite workers to ensure everything was handled properly.

The Lord gave Moses and Aaron a solemn warning to protect the Kohathite clan from destruction. If the priests were careless and left holy things exposed, the Kohathites might touch them and die. In God's eyes, the priests would be held responsible if their neglect caused a whole family to be wiped out.

To protect the Kohathites from death, the priests had to enter the sanctuary first and assign each man his exact task. Every worker was told precisely what burden to lift once the items were covered. This orderly plan prevented confusion and kept workers from wandering into dangerous contact with holy things.

The Kohathites were forbidden to look at the holy objects even for an instant while they were being wrapped. A casual or curious glance at the uncovered items would bring sudden death. This strict boundary taught Israel that God's holiness must always be approached with deep reverence.

God commanded Moses to take a census of the Gershonite clan as well. Just like the Kohathites, the men counted were between thirty and fifty years old, the prime age for heavy physical labor. They were registered to do the work of taking down and transporting the tabernacle parts assigned to them.

This statement introduces the specific duties assigned to the Gershonite families. While the Kohathites carried the sacred furniture, the Gershonites were responsible for the tabernacle curtains and fabric coverings. Their job required heavy physical labor, but it was just as vital to the worship of God as the work of the other clans.
